analysis.one_liner: Repeals limits on how many TV and radio stations one company can own and lets news outlets jointly bargain with big tech platforms.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and no action beyond its referral to the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out federal rules that cap how many broadcast stations a single company can own and that bar one company from owning both a city's main newspaper and its TV stations. It would also tell antitrust enforcers to ignore how much market share a media merger adds. On the other side of its purpose, it gives newspapers and broadcasters a four-year exemption from antitrust law so they can band together to demand payment from giant online platforms like Google and Meta. It was introduced by one senator, attracted no cosponsors, and never got a committee hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Large broadcast and newspaper companies gain the most: they could acquire unlimited stations and combine newspaper and broadcast holdings in the same market without antitrust scrutiny of their market share. Local and regional news publishers of all sizes also gain from the four-year right to collectively negotiate with the biggest online platforms for payment for their content.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large media companies and news publishers

how_it_helps.text: News publishers get a four-year safe harbor from antitrust law to jointly withhold or negotiate their content with any online platform with more than a billion monthly users, so they can bargain for payment rather than negotiate alone.
Media companies can own an unlimited number of radio and television stations, and the FCC must repeal its existing station-ownership cap.
A single company could own a daily newspaper and broadcast stations in the same market, and the FCC could not stop it.

Antitrust enforcers could not treat a media merger's added market share in TV, radio, or newspaper markets as lessening competition, effectively immunizing broadcast and newspaper consolidations from Section 7 of the Clayton Act.

analysis.who_pays: If ownership caps disappear, the cost falls on audiences in markets where one company ends up owning many stations or both the paper and the local TV news: fewer independent newsrooms, less varied local coverage, and less watchdog reporting, according to the standard rationale for the rules being repealed. The major platforms would pay in negotiations, and could pass costs on or pull news content entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news audiences and big tech platforms

drawbacks.text: Removing the FCC's ownership caps and cross-ownership ban would allow a single company to control many stations, and both the newspaper and broadcast outlets, in the same market — the exact consolidation the rules were designed to prevent.
The Clayton Act amendment tells enforcers to disregard market share from TV, radio, and newspaper mergers, shielding large media consolidations from antitrust review.

Even the collective-bargaining provision mainly benefits publishers as a class, including large chains and investment-fund owners of local papers, and conditions payment on dealing with platforms rather than fixing the underlying economics of local news.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The one provision with a plausible public benefit — letting news organizations jointly bargain with platforms that use their work for free — is bundled with a sweeping deregulation of media ownership that would concentrate local news control in fewer hands. The consolidation provisions are the bill's core; the bargaining safe harbor is bundled alongside them, and the bill never advanced far enough for anyone to weigh one against the other.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, never reaching a hearing, a vote, or the floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on September 7, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, nothing changed: large media companies did not gain the right to unlimited station ownership, and the existing ownership limits stayed in place. To the extent the bargaining safe harbor could have helped struggling local newsrooms, those publishers lost an opportunity, but no one gained a new advantage from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing ownership limits; no one gained ground

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Commerce Committee.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or moved the bill after referral, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican senator sponsored the bill with no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern emerged.

industries.note: The bill repeals the FCC's cap on how many stations one company may own and blocks antitrust review of the resulting market share, letting big station groups consolidate local markets. Fewer independent owners generally means less local news variety for viewers.

Publishers gain a four-year antitrust safe harbor to jointly negotiate payment from big platforms, which could channel money to newsrooms large and small. But the same bill lets them merge with broadcast stations in their own markets, concentrating ownership in the industry itself.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and social media companies
industries.note: Any platform with over a billion users would face coordinated negotiation and the credible threat of news publishers jointly pulling their content, raising the cost of hosting news. The impact on users depends on whether platforms pay, pass costs on, or drop news entirely.

industries.industry: Private equity and investment owners of local news chains
industries.note: The ownership deregulation opens the door to further roll-ups of financially strained local papers and stations by large holding companies, the business model most associated with cutting local newsroom staff.
